title: 03. Functions: Default Arguments
summary: Default arguments let you define a parameter with a pre-set value that is used when the caller doesn't provide that argument. They make parameters optional.
objectives: CORRECT — use None as default, create new list inside
Same problem with dict and set

sections.title: Explanation (Like You're a Junior Developer)
sections.body:
**Default arguments** let you define a parameter with a **pre-set value** that is used when the caller doesn't provide that argument. They make parameters optional.

**Real-world analogy:** When you order coffee, you don't specify "with a cup" every time — it's the default. You only specify things that differ from normal: "large", "extra shot", "oat milk". The defaults (medium size, one shot, regular milk) are assumed unless you say otherwise.

```python
def order_coffee(size="medium", shots=1, milk="regular"):
    #                 ↑             ↑          ↑
    #          defaults — used if caller doesn't specify

order_coffee()                      # All defaults used
order_coffee("large")               # Override size only
order_coffee("large", 2)            # Override size and shots
order_coffee("small", milk="oat")   # Override size and milk (skip shots)
```

**⚠️ THE MOST FAMOUS PYTHON GOTCHA — Mutable Default Arguments:**

```python
# ❌ NEVER DO THIS — shared mutable default!
def add_item(item, shopping_list=[]):
    shopping_list.append(item)
    return shopping_list

# The list [] is created ONCE when function is defined
# and REUSED across all calls!
print(add_item("apple"))   # ['apple']
print(add_item("banana"))  # ['apple', 'banana']  ← BUG! Not ['banana']!
print(add_item("cherry"))  # ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']  ← BUG!

```

# ✅ CORRECT — use None as default, create new list inside
def add_item(item, shopping_list=None):
    if shopping_list is None:
        shopping_list = []         # New list created every call
    shopping_list.append(item)
    return shopping_list

print(add_item("apple"))   # ['apple']    ✅
print(add_item("banana"))  # ['banana']   ✅
```

---

```

sections.title: 5 Examples
sections.body:
**Example 1 — Basic Default Arguments**
```python
def connect(host="localhost", port=5432, timeout=30):
    """Database connection with sensible defaults"""
    print(f"Connecting to {host}:{port} (timeout: {timeout}s)")

connect()                           # All defaults
connect("prod.db.com")             # Custom host, default port/timeout
connect("prod.db.com", 5433)       # Custom host and port
connect("prod.db.com", timeout=60) # Custom host and timeout (skip port)
connect(timeout=10)                 # Only change timeout
```

**Example 2 — The Mutable Default Gotcha (Most Asked Interview Topic!)**
```python
# ❌ WRONG — demonstrates the bug
def wrong_append(item, lst=[]):
    lst.append(item)
    return lst

print(id(wrong_append.__defaults__[0]))  # Same object every time!
print(wrong_append("a"))  # ['a']
print(wrong_append("b"))  # ['a', 'b']  ← list is shared!
print(wrong_append("c"))  # ['a', 'b', 'c']  ← still growing!

print("=" * 30)

```

# ✅ RIGHT — None pattern
def correct_append(item, lst=None):
    if lst is None:
        lst = []            # New list created fresh each call
    lst.append(item)
    return lst

print(correct_append("a"))  # ['a']
print(correct_append("b"))  # ['b']  ← fresh list!
print(correct_append("c"))  # ['c']  ← fresh list!

# ─── Same problem with dict and set ───
# ❌ Wrong
def wrong_dict(key, value, cache={}):
    cache[key] = value
    return cache

# ✅ Right
def correct_dict(key, value, cache=None):
    if cache is None:
        cache = {}
    cache[key] = value
    return cache
```

---

**Example 3 — Default Arguments with Validation**
```
```python
from datetime import datetime

def create_event(
    title,
    description="",
    start_time=None,
    duration_minutes=60,
    is_public=True,
    max_attendees=None
):
    """Create a calendar event"""
    if start_time is None:
        start_time = datetime.now()  # ✅ Correct: evaluated at call time

    if duration_minutes <= 0:
        raise ValueError("duration_minutes must be positive")

    return {
        "title": title,
        "description": description,
        "start": start_time.isoformat(),
        "duration": duration_minutes,
        "public": is_public,
        "max_attendees": max_attendees  # None = unlimited
    }

# Minimal call
event1 = create_event("Team Standup")

# Full call
event2 = create_event(
    title="Product Launch",
    description="Annual product launch event",
    start_time=datetime(2025, 6, 15, 9, 0),
    duration_minutes=120,
    is_public=True,
    max_attendees=500
)
print(event1)
print(event2)
```

**Example 4 — Overriding Defaults Selectively**
```python
def make_http_request(
    url,
    method="GET",
    headers=None,
    body=None,
    timeout=30,
    verify_ssl=True,
    follow_redirects=True,
    max_redirects=5
):
    headers = headers or {}
    print(f"{method} {url}")
    print(f"  timeout={timeout}, ssl={verify_ssl}, redirects={follow_redirects}")
    return {"status": 200, "url": url}

# GET request — all defaults perfect
make_http_request("https://api.example.com/users")

# POST request — override method and body, keep other defaults
make_http_request(
    "https://api.example.com/users",
    method="POST",
    body={"name": "Alice"},
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}
)

# Secure GET — disable redirect following
make_http_request(
    "https://secure.api.com/data",
    follow_redirects=False,
    timeout=5  # Shorter timeout
)
```

**Example 5 — Using Sentinel Objects for Defaults**
```python
# Sometimes None IS a valid value and you need to distinguish
# "not provided" from "explicitly passed None"

# Using a sentinel object
_NOT_PROVIDED = object()  # Unique sentinel — can't accidentally match

def update_user(user_id, name=_NOT_PROVIDED, email=_NOT_PROVIDED, age=_NOT_PROVIDED):
    """Only update fields that were explicitly provided"""
    updates = {}

    if name is not _NOT_PROVIDED:
        updates["name"] = name
    if email is not _NOT_PROVIDED:
        updates["email"] = email  # Can now pass email=None to clear it!
    if age is not _NOT_PROVIDED:
        updates["age"] = age

    if not updates:
        print("Nothing to update!")
        return

    print(f"Updating user {user_id}: {updates}")

update_user(42)                      # Nothing to update!
update_user(42, name="Alice")        # Updates name only
update_user(42, email=None)          # Explicitly sets email to None (clear it)
update_user(42, name="Bob", age=30)  # Updates name and age
```

quiz.explanation: 5-Year Experience Answer: "This is one of the most famous Python gotchas and a top interview question. The issue is that default argument values are evaluated ONCE — when the function is defined — not each time the function is called. For immutable defaults (numbers, strings, tuples, None), this doesn't matter because they can't change.

quiz.question: When are default argument values evaluated?
options: 5-Year Experience Answer: > > "The rule is: positional arguments must always come BEFORE keyword arguments.
5-Year Experience Answer: > > "At function definition time — not at call time.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Experience Answer: "At function definition time — not at call time. This is the core of the mutable default problem. Python evaluates each default expression exactly once when the def statement executes.
